title: Advanced Algebra
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Advanced Algebra curriculum, building on the group theory foundation of MTH300 and the ring/field foundation of MTH306: group actions and Sylow theory beyond basic group axioms/subgroups/Lagrange, followed by ring theory (ideals, quotient rings, integral domains, PIDs/UFDs), polynomial rings, field extensions, finite fields, and an introduction to modules. Content deliberately avoids repeating MTH300's basic group-axiom material.

questions.question: A group action of a group G on a set X is a map G times X to X satisfying:
options: e times x = x for the identity e, and (gh) times x = g times (h times x) for all g,h in G, x in X
g times x = x for all g
g times x = e for all x
questions.correct_answer: e times x = x for the identity e, and (gh) times x = g times (h times x) for all g,h in G, x in X
questions.explanation: These two axioms define a group action, generalizing how permutations or symmetries act on a set.

questions.question: The orbit of an element x under a group action of G is defined as:
questions.explanation: The orbit collects all elements reachable from x under the action of every group element.

questions.question: The stabilizer of an element x under a group action is defined as:
options: {g in G : g times x = x}
questions.correct_answer: {g in G : g times x = x}
questions.explanation: The stabilizer consists of exactly those group elements that fix x, and it forms a subgroup of G.

questions.question: The Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem states that for a finite group G acting on a set X and x in X:
questions.explanation: This theorem relates the size of a group to the sizes of an orbit and its corresponding stabilizer subgroup.

questions.question: A group G acting on itself by conjugation partitions G into equivalence classes called:
questions.explanation: Conjugation is a group action of G on itself, and its orbits are precisely the conjugacy classes.

questions.question: The center Z(G) of a group G, consisting of elements commuting with every element of G, is:
options: Equal to G only if G is trivial
questions.explanation: The center is always a normal subgroup, since conjugating a central element by any group element leaves it unchanged.

questions.question: For a prime p, a Sylow p-subgroup of a finite group G is defined as:
options: A subgroup of order p^n, where p^n is the highest power of p dividing |G|
Any subgroup whose order is a multiple of p
questions.correct_answer: A subgroup of order p^n, where p^n is the highest power of p dividing |G|
questions.explanation: Sylow p-subgroups are maximal p-subgroups of G, with order exactly the largest power of p dividing |G|.

questions.question: Sylow's First Theorem guarantees that for a finite group G and prime p dividing |G|:
options: At least one Sylow p-subgroup exists
Every subgroup is a Sylow subgroup
questions.correct_answer: At least one Sylow p-subgroup exists
questions.explanation: This existence theorem is the starting point of Sylow theory, guaranteeing subgroups of the maximal prime-power order.

questions.question: Sylow's Third Theorem states that the number of Sylow p-subgroups, n_p, satisfies:
options: n_p is congruent to 1 modulo p, and n_p divides |G|/p^n
questions.correct_answer: n_p is congruent to 1 modulo p, and n_p divides |G|/p^n
questions.explanation: This congruence and divisibility condition strongly constrains the possible number of Sylow p-subgroups.

questions.question: A group is called simple if:
options: Its only normal subgroups are the trivial subgroup and the group itself
questions.correct_answer: Its only normal subgroups are the trivial subgroup and the group itself
questions.explanation: Simple groups are the building blocks of finite group theory, analogous to prime numbers in arithmetic.

questions.question: A composition series of a group G is a chain of subgroups where each is a normal subgroup of the next, and each successive quotient is:
questions.explanation: The composition factors (successive quotients) of a composition series are simple groups, and by the Jordan-Holder theorem this list is essentially unique.

questions.question: The external direct product G times H of two groups G and H, with componentwise operation, has order:
questions.explanation: Each element of the direct product is an ordered pair, so the total count is the product of the individual group orders.

questions.question: A ring (R, +, times) is an algebraic structure in which (R, +) is an abelian group and multiplication is:
options: Commutative only, with no other requirement
questions.explanation: These are the minimal axioms required of multiplication in a ring, beyond the additive abelian group structure.

questions.question: A commutative ring with unity that has no zero divisors is called:
questions.explanation: Integral domains generalize the arithmetic of the integers, where the product of two nonzero elements is never zero.

questions.question: A field is a commutative ring with unity in which:
options: Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse
questions.correct_answer: Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse
questions.explanation: This invertibility condition on all nonzero elements is what distinguishes a field from a general ring or integral domain.

questions.question: Every field is automatically:
options: A group under multiplication including zero
questions.explanation: Since every nonzero element of a field is invertible, a product of nonzero elements cannot be zero, satisfying the integral domain property.

questions.question: A subset I of a ring R is called an ideal if:
options: I is an additive subgroup of R, and rI is contained in I and Ir is contained in I for all r in R
I is any subring of R
questions.correct_answer: I is an additive subgroup of R, and rI is contained in I and Ir is contained in I for all r in R
questions.explanation: An ideal must absorb multiplication by any ring element, a stronger condition than just being a subring.

questions.question: The quotient ring R/I, for an ideal I of R, consists of:
options: Cosets r + I with addition and multiplication induced from R
questions.correct_answer: Cosets r + I with addition and multiplication induced from R
questions.explanation: The ideal property ensures that multiplication of cosets is well defined, making R/I a ring in its own right.

questions.question: An ideal M of a ring R is called maximal if:
options: M is not equal to R, and there is no ideal strictly between M and R
questions.correct_answer: M is not equal to R, and there is no ideal strictly between M and R
questions.explanation: Maximal ideals are the largest proper ideals possible, with no other ideal fitting strictly between them and the whole ring.

questions.question: If M is a maximal ideal of a commutative ring R with unity, then the quotient ring R/M is:
options: An integral domain but never a field
questions.explanation: Maximality of M is exactly the condition needed for R/M to have every nonzero element invertible.

questions.question: An ideal P of a commutative ring R is called prime if P is not equal to R and whenever the product ab lies in P:
options: Either a is in P or b is in P
Both a and b must be in P
Neither a nor b is in P
questions.correct_answer: Either a is in P or b is in P
questions.explanation: This condition generalizes the notion of a prime number's defining property to ideals of a general ring.

questions.question: If P is a prime ideal of a commutative ring R with unity, then R/P is:
questions.explanation: Primality of P exactly corresponds to R/P having no zero divisors, i.e. being an integral domain.

questions.question: A ring homomorphism phi: R to S is a map that preserves:
questions.explanation: A ring homomorphism must respect both of the ring's operations to be a structure-preserving map.

questions.question: The kernel of a ring homomorphism phi: R to S is always:
questions.explanation: The kernel absorbs multiplication by elements of R, satisfying the defining property of an ideal, and R/ker(phi) is isomorphic to the image of phi.

questions.question: A principal ideal domain (PID) is an integral domain in which:
options: Every ideal is generated by a single element
Every ideal has infinitely many generators
There are no ideals at all
questions.correct_answer: Every ideal is generated by a single element
questions.explanation: PIDs are integral domains with the strong structural property that all their ideals are principal, i.e. generated by one element.

questions.question: A unique factorization domain (UFD) is an integral domain in which every nonzero non-unit element:
options: Can be written as a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and units
questions.correct_answer: Can be written as a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and units
questions.explanation: This generalizes the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (unique prime factorization of integers) to a broader class of rings.

questions.question: The ring of polynomials F[x] over a field F is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Because F[x] has a division algorithm, every ideal is generated by a single polynomial (the one of least degree in the ideal), making it a PID.

questions.question: A polynomial p(x) over a field F is called irreducible if:
options: It cannot be factored into a product of two polynomials of lower positive degree over F
It has no roots in F
questions.correct_answer: It cannot be factored into a product of two polynomials of lower positive degree over F
questions.explanation: Irreducible polynomials play the role of primes within the polynomial ring, forming the basis of unique factorization there.

questions.question: A field extension K of a field F is called algebraic if every element of K:
options: Is a root of some nonzero polynomial with coefficients in F
questions.correct_answer: Is a root of some nonzero polynomial with coefficients in F
questions.explanation: This is the defining property of an algebraic extension, contrasting with transcendental extensions.

questions.question: An element that is not algebraic over a field F is called:
questions.explanation: Transcendental elements, such as pi over the rational numbers, satisfy no nonzero polynomial equation with coefficients in F.

questions.question: The degree [K:F] of a field extension K over F is defined as:
options: The dimension of K as a vector space over F
The number of elements in K
The number of subfields of K
questions.correct_answer: The dimension of K as a vector space over F
questions.explanation: Since K is naturally a vector space over F, its degree is defined as this vector space dimension.

questions.question: For any prime p and positive integer n, there exists a unique (up to isomorphism) finite field with:
questions.explanation: This classification theorem for finite fields shows that every finite field has prime-power order and is essentially unique for that order.

questions.question: A module over a ring R generalizes the notion of a vector space by replacing the field of scalars with:
questions.explanation: Modules extend the vector space concept by allowing scalars from any ring rather than requiring a field, giving up guaranteed properties like bases.
